channel.title: BotsDoThat: new AI agent use cases
channel.description: A live, sourced feed of real things people hand to AI agents (inbox and phone calls, shopping, travel, family, health, work, small business), with real popularity numbers, plain-English guides, copy-paste prompts, build-your-own-bot blueprints and tips to run your bots for less.

item.title: Build a second brain your bot reads every morning
item.description: Keep your notes, plans and to-dos in plain files you own, plus one short "about me" file. Your bot reads them at the start of every chat, so it remembers who you are and picks up where you left off. You end up with: An assistant that remembers your life and work across days, with all of that memory sitting in a folder you control.

item.title: Have two AIs check each other's answers
item.description: Before you trust an important answer, have your bot ask a second AI the same question, compare the two, and check the real sources itself. Each AI catches mistakes the other missed. You end up with: A double-checked answer with sources, instead of one AI's best guess.

item.title: Fill out a job application faster with an agent
item.description: Online job applications ask for the same details over and over. A browser agent can type them in from your resume and a short fact sheet, while you sign in yourself and press Submit yourself. You end up with: An application filled in from your own facts, a list of anything the agent couldn't answer, and a summary to check before you press Submit.

item.title: Let your bot handle your website's contact email
item.description: Forward the contact address of your website, club or class to your bot's own email. It reads each message, sums it up for you, and only answers when you say so. You end up with: One short summary instead of a cluttered contact inbox, with replies drafted and waiting for your OK.

item.title: Set spend limits and usage alerts on your AI accounts
item.description: Before a bot runs on autopilot, put a hard cap on what it can spend and check usage weekly, so a runaway loop can't run up a big bill. You end up with: A known worst-case monthly bill, and an early warning when a bot starts using more than expected.

item.title: Keep your bot's prompts, tools and context short
item.description: You pay for everything the model reads on every run: your instructions, tool definitions, pasted pages and the conversation so far. Trimming those is often the easiest saving. You end up with: Smaller, faster runs that cost less, with the same results.

item.title: Stop always-on bots from burning tokens: run them less often, or on demand
item.description: Every scheduled run costs tokens, even when nothing has changed. Match the schedule to how often the thing really changes, and switch fun-but-idle bots to run only when you ask. You end up with: The same alerts and reports with far fewer paid runs.

item.title: Run open models on your own computer (or a cheap host) for simple jobs
item.description: Open-weight models can run on your own computer with a free tool like Ollama, so routine jobs cost nothing per message. Some hosts also run open models for a fraction of big-model prices. You end up with: Routine bot jobs that run on your own hardware with no per-message bill, and your private text staying on your machine.

item.title: Cut your AI bill with prompt caching and batch discounts
item.description: If your bot sends the same long instructions every time, caching makes the repeat part much cheaper. If results can wait a few hours, batch processing halves the price at several providers. You end up with: The same bot output, with repeated instructions billed at a fraction of the input price and non-urgent work at half price.

item.title: Decide between a monthly AI plan and paying per use
item.description: A monthly plan (like Claude Pro) gives you a flat price with usage limits. Paying per use through an API costs exactly what you use. Which is cheaper depends on how much your bots run. You end up with: A clear answer for your own usage: stay on a plan, switch to pay-per-use, or mix both.

item.title: Build and test your bot on a free tier before you pay
item.description: Several AI providers let you try their API or app for free. Use that to prove your bot works before you put a card on file, and know what you give up on the free tier. You end up with: A bot you know works, a realistic cost estimate, and no surprise bill while you were experimenting.

item.title: Use a small model for simple jobs and save the big one for hard ones
item.description: Most bot jobs (sorting email, summarizing, checking a page) don't need the most powerful model. The small models cost a fraction as much, so route easy work to them and only send hard problems up. You end up with: The same results on everyday jobs for a fraction of the cost, with the expensive model kept for the jobs that need it.

item.title: Send a long video or thread to your bot with one reply
item.description: See a long video or X thread you don't have time for? Reply to it by tagging your bot, and a short summary waits for you in your bot's app later. You end up with: A read-later pile of short summaries, saved without copying links or leaving the app you were scrolling.

item.title: Hand a clunky web form or app to an agent that uses the computer for you
item.description: Some software you only touch once a year. A computer-use agent can click through it for you, from a login you control, while you watch. You end up with: The form filled in correctly without you learning the software, ready for your final click.

item.title: Get roadside help abroad when nobody speaks your language
item.description: Broken down in another country and the insurer's phone line is in a language you don't speak? An agent can find the right help form, fill it in with your details and get help moving. You end up with: A roadside-assistance request filed in the local system, and a plain summary of what comes next.

item.title: Give your bot a phone number so it can call and book for you
item.description: Plenty of places still only take bookings by phone. Once your bot has its own number, it can call a restaurant, a vet or a salon, book the slot and tell you what was said. You end up with: A booking made by phone, a plain summary of the call and a calendar entry, without you making the call.

item.title: Have an agent research a used car from its listing link
item.description: Drop in a used-car listing link and let an agent dig in: what the model is known for, the car's damage history and the questions to ask before you call the seller. You end up with: A one-page report on the car, its history and what to ask, before you spend time on a viewing.

item.title: Send all your newsletters to your bot and get one daily report
item.description: Subscribe your newsletters to your bot's own email address. It reads every issue and sends you one short report each day, with a score that tells you which ones are worth reading in full. You end up with: One daily digest in place of a pile of unread newsletters, and a clear signal about which subscriptions earn their place.

item.title: Give your agents their own Apple account so they share reminders, notes and calendar
item.description: A Mac signed in to a separate Apple Account can become the shared desk where your agents leave each other reminders, notes, calendar events and messages, while your personal account stays private. You end up with: A shared to-do list, notebook and calendar your agents all use, kept apart from your own account.

item.title: Put a small team of agents on one project, each with its own job
item.description: Instead of one chatbot doing everything, give separate agents separate roles (one researches, one builds) and let them hand work to each other in a shared conversation you can watch. You end up with: One finished piece of work (in the source, a simple website) built from a research step and a build step, with every hand-off visible.

item.title: Hand off tasks to your agent by voice while you drive
item.description: Long drive? Talk to your agent on a voice call and hand off research, follow-ups and to-dos, then find them done when you arrive. You end up with: A list of tasks started or finished during the drive, waiting for your review.

item.title: Get pinged when a prescription is ready, and told when to leave
item.description: A personal agent can sweep your email every morning for "ready for pickup" notices, and check live traffic before your appointments to tell you when to head out. You end up with: A ping when your prescription is ready and a "leave now" nudge before each appointment.

item.title: Have an agent contact tradespeople and line up quotes for a home project
item.description: Instead of calling round electricians, plumbers and roofers yourself, let an agent reach out to all of them, collect their replies and put them side by side. You end up with: One table of replies from every trade, so you can pick who to meet.

item.title: Write a letter of recommendation for someone
item.description: Someone asked you for a reference letter and you want it to sound specific and honest, not generic. AI can turn your notes and their resume into a solid first draft. You end up with: A one-page letter with real examples of the person's work, written in your voice, ready for you to sign and send.

item.title: Log your meals by talking and get a daily weight check-in
item.description: Tell your bot what you ate, out loud, and it keeps the food log for you. It can also check in on your weight each morning. You end up with: A food and weight log that fills itself in, without typing into a tracking app.

item.title: Have your bot make a customer-service phone call for you
item.description: Some jobs still need a phone call, like cancelling a service or sorting out an account. With a phone-calling add-on, your bot can make the call, sit on hold and report back. You end up with: The call handled (for example, a service cancelled), a plain summary of what was said and any confirmation number, without you sitting on hold.

item.title: Get your phone number off people-search sites to cut spam calls
item.description: A bot finds where your phone number is listed on people-search and data-broker sites, files the opt-out requests, and checks again later. You end up with: A list of where your number was listed, opt-outs filed, and a regular re-check.

item.title: Have a bot watch any web page and ping you when it changes
item.description: Instead of refreshing a page, tell a bot what matters on it. It checks on a schedule and pings you only when that changes. You end up with: One ping when it matters, and no more refreshing.

item.title: Let an agent reorder your regular groceries
item.description: Some people now let an agent handle their weekly grocery order and switch stores when a better offer appears. You end up with: Groceries ordered after a quick chat and one confirm tap.

item.title: Plan and book a whole trip by texting your bot
item.description: One parent says his bot booked the flight, the rental car, the vacation rental, a restaurant and event tickets, all over text. You end up with: A booked trip with every confirmation in one chat.

item.title: Get a daily scam check on your inbox
item.description: A read-only bot reads your new email each morning and gives each suspicious message a risk score and the red flags. You end up with: A morning list: “Confirmed scam / High suspicion / Possible / Clear”, with what to do next.

item.title: Give your agent its own email address
item.description: Give your agent an inbox of its own. Then you or anyone else can forward it jobs, like a meeting request it turns into a calendar invite with prep notes. You end up with: A forwarding address for chores. Forward it a request and it gets handled.

item.title: Run family logistics from the family group chat
item.description: New “family agents” sit in your family chat and handle the small jobs: restocking, booking the dentist and reminders. You end up with: Fewer “did anyone book…?” messages, and one place where family requests get done.

item.title: Set up medication and appointment reminders for a parent
item.description: Family agents can remind an older parent about medication and book routine appointments, with the family kept in the loop. You end up with: Reminders that actually reach Mum or Dad, and a family that knows they did.

item.title: Get a Monday recap of your inbox and a to-do list
item.description: Every Monday a bot reviews last week's email, recaps what matters and suggests a ranked to-do list. You end up with: A 2-minute Monday briefing and a ranked to-do list.

item.title: Get a 2-minute morning digest on topics you care about
item.description: A bot reads the news on your topics every morning and sends you a short plain-English digest, or even an audio version. You end up with: A short daily briefing instead of doom-scrolling.

item.title: Catch family calendar clashes before the week starts
item.description: Every Sunday a bot reads the next two weeks of your family calendar and school notices and flags the clashes. You end up with: A short Sunday note: what's coming up, what clashes, and what to prepare.

item.title: Keep a household essentials list and reorder on time
item.description: A bot keeps a running list of essentials, asks once a week what's low and builds the reorder. You end up with: No more running out of toilet paper or lunchbox snacks.

item.title: Get 5 weekend activity ideas that fit your kids and the weather
item.description: Every Friday, get activity ideas matched to your kids' ages, the weather and your budget, with a rainy-day backup. You end up with: A Friday list of 5 doable weekend plans.

item.title: Get your ads and sales numbers every morning without logging in
item.description: A bot logs into your ad and sales dashboards (read-only) and sends a morning summary with what changed. You end up with: A 1-minute morning report instead of 5 dashboards.
